# Catch up: shop, 1.5.2.dev0 to 1.5.2.dev0

`slipwai migrate` wrote this before it returned — whether the merge committed or stopped at conflicts — from the catch-up note in each version's entry in the factory's own `CHANGELOG.md`, written by whoever made the change, in the commit that made it. It is what a merge could not do for you.

Work it with `/catch-up`, which reads this file and runs `make verify` against it. This file is git-ignored and disposable: delete it when the work is done, and the changelog stays the record.

## Why the versions crossed could not be listed as such

Because `1.5.2.dev0` and `1.5.2.dev0` are both 1.5.2 — a snapshot of that release, or the release itself — and the changelog keeps one entry per release, so what changed between the two is not told apart. The 1.5.2 entry as it stands today is below; the part of it this project already had cannot be separated from the part it has just taken, so read it as a whole.

## The one entry both versions belong to, 1.5.2

### 1.5.2 — PATCH

`check-imports`, `check-migrations` and `check-codegraph` stop reading what the answer never needed. `adopt --refresh` (experimental: brownfield adoption) no longer rewrites the four files a project owns. `adopt --refresh`, `--confirm` and `--decline` (experimental: brownfield adoption) now refuse to write over an uncommitted change where the project sits in a subdirectory of its git repository. `check-slice-scope` compares a slice branch with the trunk's own refs, so a branch no longer empties its own check by minting a base. `check-slice-scope` no longer refuses a slice's own code in a repository adopted at its root (`adopt`, experimental), and a slice id with a slug is read whole.

**Owes:** A repository already adopted in a subdirectory may meet one refusal, once. If an earlier run left regenerated files uncommitted, nothing was recorded for them, and the first refresh, confirm or decline after this change refuses, naming them, because slipwai cannot tell them from an edit of yours. Commit the files it names and run it again; where the list ends in "and N more", type `git add -A . && git commit` in the project's directory, which commits everything uncommitted under the project, and run it again; nothing else is asked. Do not stash them: a stash takes the answers you have settled in `project.json` with it, and the refusal returns after `git stash pop`. The refusal now also says where its names are spelled from: the project's directory, which is not the repository's top when the project sits in a subdirectory. `slipwai migrate` carries the corrected script; nothing else in a repository changes. Two things you may see afterwards. On a developer's machine, a slice branch with no trunk to compare with — no `main` ref, or a shallow clone too short to reach the branch point — used to pass as "nothing to hold"; it now fails with a single line that names the command to run (`git fetch origin <trunk>:refs/remotes/origin/<trunk>`, or `git fetch --unshallow origin`); the longer form is there because a bare `git fetch origin <trunk>` in a single-branch clone leaves no ref for the check to find. In any CI run with no trunk to compare with — a pull-request checkout, which is depth 1 by default, or a run with `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS` or `GITLAB_CI` set — the check still exits 0 and now says on stderr that the slice was NOT checked. A maintainer who wants it held there adds `fetch-depth: 0` to the verify job's checkout (`GIT_DEPTH: "0"` on GitLab). A local shell with one of those variables set gets the same line instead of the failure.

## Then

`make verify`. A gate that is new in one of the versions above fails code that was correct when it was written; the entry that introduced it says what it now wants instead. Never edit a gate to make it pass — it came from the factory, the next migration brings it back, and a locally softened copy is a false green until then.
